description_intent: Windows Installer keeps a single scripting-safety switch it checks before carrying out an install request that originated from script content rather than a person directly launching a package. Left in its restrictive position, that switch means a script-triggered install request still surfaces a confirmation prompt asking whether to proceed, rather than the script's own say-so being treated as enough to move straight to installation.
rationale_intent: The confirmation dialog exists specifically to put a human decision between 'a webpage asked to install something' and 'software actually landed on this device' - it is the one point where an install driven by content the user never deliberately sought out gets a chance to be recognized and refused. A single browsing session can load script from dozens of origins, most of them outside any relationship the organization vetted, so removing that checkpoint would make 'did a script ask' the deciding factor for whether code gets installed, instead of 'did the person in front of the screen agree' - a distinction that matters far more once ordinary browsing routinely touches the open internet than it did when this setting was first written for a smaller, more contained set of sites.
